question: I want to measure the distance between two Bluetooth devices (A Master and a slave) using the corresponding RSSI value. Is there any algorithm or popular approach that maps RSSI values directly to distance?

sections.title: Fundamental Principles and Limitations
sections.text: Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI) quantifies the actual signal power received by a device, typically expressed in decibel milliwatts (dBm) [1]. While RSSI can measure the distance between a transmitter and receiver based on the difference between transmitted and received signal power [1], it does not provide an exact distance measurement. Instead, it offers an approximation that relies on specific propagation models to convert signal strength into spatial data [1]. It is noted that some literature does not strictly distinguish between receive power, pathloss, and RSSI, which can complicate precise modeling.

sections.title: Propagation and Geometric Models
sections.text: Two primary propagation models are generally used to convert RSSI to distance: free-space models and log-normal models [1]. In a pure free-space scenario, power loss is proportional to the square of the distance (d) between the transmitter and receiver [3]. More generally, this pathloss is modeled as d raised to the power of n_PL, where n_PL is a pathloss coefficient that depends on the specific environment and whether a line-of-sight (LOS) connection exists [3]. Geometric approaches utilize these adequate models to calculate distances directly from RSSI values [1]. Alternatively, a Signal Propagation Model can predict distance by performing a power regression against a known table of distances and corresponding RSSI values [2].

question: In auditory speech perception using iEEG, I will use Temporal Response Function (TRF) to determine correlations between stimulus characteristics (variations in the acoustic signal envelope, for example) and characteristics of recorded neuronal activity. I would like to fully understand the different stages of data processing carried out, as well as the reasoning and hypotheses behind them.

sections.title: Theoretical Foundations and Hypotheses
sections.text: The Temporal Response Function (TRF) framework posits that the brain processes speech through ascending stages, where emergent features evolve from acoustic to sentence-level linguistic representations as incremental steps [3]. This approach addresses the limitations of traditional EEG methods, which fail to provide a comprehensive measure of how the brain tracks multidimensional prosodic aspects over time [1]. By measuring neural entrainment to the speech envelope, researchers can target prosodic processing, a domain that remains underutilized in the literature [1]. Prosodic cues, which communicate information through acoustic correlates such as duration, amplitude, and fundamental frequency, are indispensable for comprehending messages, recognizing emotion, and parsing syntax [1]. These cues may scaffold linguistic processing by supporting neural synchronization to the speech envelope [1]. The extraction of amplitude modulation (AM) information is considered a fundamental procedure within the auditory neural architecture [1], and the auditory cortex is particularly adept at rapidly processing spectro-temporal changes in temporal fine structure [1]. Furthermore, neural tracking of the temporal envelope has been applied to study speech segmentation, where the envelope is mapped onto neural activity [2]. Exaggerated speech signals, characterized by louder, longer, and higher-pitched stressed syllables, facilitate the segmentation of speech into syllable units and the disentangling of word boundaries [1]. This framework is also relevant for clinical populations; for instance, the prosodic phrasing hypothesis suggests that children with developmental language disorder (DLD) have difficulty detecting rhythmic patterns due to impaired sensitivity to amplitude rise time and sound duration [1].

sections.title: Mathematical Modeling and Estimation
sections.text: The TRF is defined as an unknown, channel-specific filter that describes the linear transformation of the ongoing stimulus into ongoing EEG activity [1] [5]. In this forward modeling approach, the instantaneous neural activity r(t,n) is modeled as the convolution of the acoustic stimulation s(t), specifically the speech envelope, with this unknown channel-specific TRF [5]. The mapping of the speech stimulus to the neural network via this linear transformation allows for the identification of neural signals related to auditory processing, effectively acting as an additional preprocessing stage [4]. The TRF is a continuous signal that exhibits the neural encoding of speech features over time, typically spanning hundreds of milliseconds [3]. Peaks of different latencies within this signal indicate separate processing stages, analogous to event-related potentials (ERPs) [3] [2]. To estimate the model weights, the mean absolute difference between the actual neural response r(t) and the predicted response r̂(t) is minimized, where the prediction error is denoted as ε(t). This method solves the issue of temporal smearing, which creates noise in simple cross-correlation functions due to averaging across time points [1]. In the backward direction, recording channels are weighted based on the information they provide for reconstruction, which removes inter-channel redundancies [1]. The fine-grained time resolution provided by techniques like MEG offers insight into the temporal progression of these cascading neural processes.

sections.title: Data Processing and Validation Pipeline
sections.text: Invasive EEG (iEEG) data, acquired using subdural electrode grids or depth electrodes, differs from typical scalp EEG (10-20 system). A similar preprocessing pipeline has been selected for a variety of studies using TRF to investigate auditory processing [4]. Researchers often choose minimal preprocessing on the EEG signal, excluding common steps like independent component analysis (ICA), because the data will be further processed using the TRF [4]. In specific implementations, data analyses are performed in mne-python 0.23.0 and eelbrain 0.36, where flat channels are excluded and environmental magnetic interferences are suppressed using temporal signal space separation (tSSS). For validation, a 4-fold cross-validation strategy is employed; for each testing fold, the remaining three partitions serve as validation sets to generate three TRFs, which are then averaged to one TRF per fold. Prediction accuracy is computed against the testing set, and both TRFs and accuracies are further averaged across folds. To ensure unbiased comparison, TRFs are generated from the same number of predictors, and peaks are identified and compared across passage types using repeated measures ANOVA and FDR-corrected t-tests. Experimental configurations typically involve specific numbers of blocks, total trials per participant, trials per passage type, and stimulus passage durations, with inclusion criteria often requiring at least 70% correct on comprehension questions [C7-C11, C31]. Stimulus delivery levels are also controlled. Other iEEG processing examples include using power spectral density (PSD) over 3-second windows per channel pair as input to a two-state Hidden Markov Model (HMM) for mapping iEEG to normal or peri-ictal states, with parameters estimated via Baum-Welch. Alternatively, feature extraction may involve a 7-level stationary wavelet transform (SWT) leading to codebook vector quantization, using Baum-Welch for parameter estimation and Viterbi for recognition. The stimulus reconstruction approach has also been tested in four-speaker free field environments for auditory attention decoding [5].

question: In robotics, what are the leading methods for learning terrain traversibility costs automatically from robot experience?

sections.title: Experience-Based Autonomous Learning
sections.text: A primary approach involves robots autonomously determining which terrains are traversable based on prior navigation experience, without relying on external sources [3]. This experiential learning framework addresses robotic navigation by learning how to traverse real-world environments directly from real-world data [2]. The process is structured into two levels: a low level that deals with local traversibility and a high level that determines which paths are more likely to lead to the destination [2]. A key motivation for this approach is that it is difficult to accurately estimate a terrain's actual cost until the robot traverses it itself, highlighting the importance of learning from previous experience [1].

To estimate terrain traversability cost, the robot needs to fuse color data (terrain texture), depth data (identifying non-traversable regions like obstacles), and proprioceptive feedback (implicitly encoding the physics) in real time and the real world.

sections.title: Proprioceptive and Energy-Based Metrics
sections.text: Several methods utilize robot proprioceptive features to characterize specific traversal costs. Faigl and Prágr use these features to define three costs: mean instantaneous power consumption, mean forward velocity, and attitude stability, which are then attached to exteroceptive features for regression [5]. In a related unsupervised approach, Faigl and Prágr adopt a method for traversability cost maps regression [4]. Similarly, self-organizing maps are proposed to predict these same three traversal costs—instantaneous power consumption, maximum achievable forward velocity, and attitude stability—based on terrain morphology and appearance captured by an RGB-D camera [4]. During the learning phase, the predicting model is fed with the traversal costs actually experienced by the robot during traversal to refine these estimates [4].

question: In recommendation systems, how are new methods that optimize diversity typically evaluated?

sections.title: Multi-Dimensional Evaluation Frameworks
sections.text: Assessing recommendation systems requires moving beyond traditional accuracy metrics like RMSE and P@N to include diversity, novelty, and serendipity. These newer concepts are considered orthogonal to accuracy and have been shown to increase user satisfaction [2]. Recent reviews emphasize evaluating performance from multiple perspectives, including accuracy, diversity, and novelty, while analyzing the advantages, disadvantages, and applicable environments of specific metrics [1]. Furthermore, predictions regarding the future development direction of these evaluation metrics are part of the ongoing scholarly discourse [1]. In graph neural network-based systems, beyond-accuracy aspects such as diversity, serendipity, and fairness are recognized as key influencers of user engagement, highlighting the critical accuracy-diversity trade-off.

sections.title: Hierarchical Diversity Objectives
sections.text: Diversity is conceptualized at three distinct levels: user-level, item-level, and system-level [1]. A significant finding is that systems optimized for user- or item-level diversity do not necessarily perform well in system-level diversity [4]. This discrepancy motivates the development of new objectives that combine all three considerations to ensure holistic performance [4]. At the system level, metrics like P-Coverage focus on measuring the fraction of items recommended, a factor closely related to cold-start issues. Additionally, Adomavicius and Kwon utilized the total number of different items recommended across all users as an aggregate diversity measure to evaluate algorithms [3].

sections.text: Diversity metrics are often categorized into relevance-oblivious and relevance-aware types, with specific measures including NRBP, nDCU@K, M-IA, D-M, and D#-M. Common calculation methods involve using item-item similarity based on content to form neighborhoods, then measuring the min, max, sum, or average distance between item pairs [3]. Another approach, proposed by Ziegler et al., measures the value of inserting a new item into the recommendation list [3]. ILAD and ILMD are defined as the mean and minimum dissimilarity of all pairs within a list, respectively. ILAD and ILMD are defined as the mean and minimum dissimilarity of all pairs within a list, respectively .
Diversity metrics are often categorized into relevance-oblivious and relevance-aware types, with specific measures including NRBP, nDCU@K, M-IA, D-M, and D#-M .
A typical three-stage process involves generating top-k items via item-CF, creating bi-objective Pareto top-s lists, and re-ranking the results .
To balance accuracy and diversity, multi-objective optimization techniques such as NNIA, AMOSA, and NSGA-II are employed .

sections.title: Theoretical Foundations and Limitations
sections.text: The Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem traditionally dictates that the sampling frequency must not be less than twice the maximum frequency of the signal to be recorded [2]. This principle establishes that a function containing no frequencies above half the sampling rate can be perfectly reconstructed. However, this theorem provides only a sufficient upper boundary for the sampling rate, rather than an absolute limit on information recovery. Consequently, research has emerged addressing the possibility of obtaining frequency domain information beyond these standard constraints [1].

sections.title: Exploiting Aliasing and Undersampling
sections.text: One approach to surpassing traditional limits involves the advantageous use of aliasing for measurements above the Nyquist frequency [4]. This is achieved by repeating measurements in various frequency bands and merging the resulting data [4]. The frequency translation aspect of aliasing can be specifically exploited through techniques known as undersampling, band-pass sampling, harmonic sampling, or Super-Nyquist sampling [3]. While effective, this technique is constrained by the requirement that the frequency limit of the aliased data must remain below a specific threshold.

sections.title: Control Theory and Signal Reconstruction
sections.text: Sampled-data control theory offers a method to reconstruct lost high-frequency components that lie beyond the so-called Nyquist frequency [6]. This approach allows for the recovery of higher frequency content without relying on the Restricted Isometry Property (RIP) [4]. Specifically, J. Javh et al. demonstrated that exciting a structure in a predetermined frequency band enables the recovery of these higher frequency components [4]. Additionally, a trust-region algorithm has been developed to minimize a smoothed non-convex least-squares objective function, allowing for the iterative recovery of the underlying signal of interest for either time- or band-limited support [5].

sections.title: Practical Constraints and Excitation Challenges
sections.text: Despite these advancements, pure sinusoidal excitation remains a severe limitation because many single-frequency measurements are required to fully describe a wide frequency range [1]. This challenge is exacerbated in frequency bands with a high density of natural modes, where the component response strongly depends on the specific excitation frequency [1]. In such dense modal environments, even slight variations in frequency can determine significant changes in the response [1]. To address temporal dynamics, efficient sampling schemes are discussed to obtain both the frequency spectrum and signal energy [7]. Furthermore, in the time domain, if the signal is repeatable and its phase is manipulable, performing repetitions with different phases represents a feasible approach for data acquisition [4].
